title: About the Parakeet King in Boy and the Heron…

commenti.body:
I agree it’s a fantastic film. I think it’s one that’s going to need several rewatches and some research to really understand on a deep level. My impression was there was a great deal of multi-level symbolism going on throughout and some of that, particularly around the birthing room and the politics of the Parakeets, is going to need some cultural insight I just don’t have to make sense of. 

Anyway, I think it’s clear at least that the Parakeet King smashed the stones in the end because he was angry and ignorant of how is world worked. He just lashed out in ignorance and ended up destroying his world. That’s a pretty pointed message, I think. 

Also, it seems like you missed the thread with the whole family. The grand uncle has been drawing family members there in order to find a successor, and also the place has a unique relationship with time itself. His younger mother is his actual mother from the past, in the year she disappeared into the tower. She was there for the same reason he was, to be evaluated as a potential successor. 

But the birthing room, I’ve got nothing. I’d wager there’s some Japanese tradition there that’s gone over my head.

I assumed that that was the reason about why he slashed the stones but I just wanted to make sure. 

That makes sense about why she would be there in the first place but why did she stay? Based on context provided by Kiriko, it seemed like she had been there for a very long time. I wouldn’t think it would take many years to evaluate. In this world alternate world I assume time in the above is irrelevant so that explains why they are both there simultaneously. I still don’t understand why the parakeets would kidnap his Mom and present her to the granduncle if he was already evaluating her. Why would they prefer she be the successor and not Mahito? I also read that the Parakeets were based off of Mussolini and his troops.
If time from the above was irrelevant however, why was Mahito’s grandmother not in the alternate world with him and his Mom?

I interpret the tower, which came into existence shortly before the Meiji Restoration, as a metaphor for the then-modern Japanese state, in its death throes by the time of the film as a result of WW2. In that lens, the parakeets who infest the tower and are "gaining leverage" over its master are the Japanese militarists, depicted as an importation of European fascism.
